events.title: So Others May Live: Army Aeromedical Evacuation Operations in the Republic of Vietnam, 1962-1973
events.venue: National Museum of Health and Medicine
events.description: During the Vietnam War, “Dustoff” became the name for helicopter medical evacuation missions that transformed battlefield medicine. Beginning with the first five Huey helicopters deployed to Vietnam, unarmed Dustoff crews evacuated more than 900,000 wounded and injured between 1962 and 1973. Their work helped wounded service members reach lifesaving care within the critical “golden hour” after injury. Join Donald Hall, Ph.D., as he explores the history, innovation, and lasting impact of Dustoff and the evolution of battlefield medical evacuation during the Vietnam War.

events.title: The Catholic University of America Symphony Orchestra in Concert
events.venue: St. Andrew the Apostle Catholic Church
events.description: On Sunday, November 15, at 4:00 PM, the St. Andrew the Apostle Concert Series proudly welcomes The Catholic University of America Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Maestro Simeone Tartaglione, for a free afternoon of orchestral masterworks. Program Paul Dukas – The Sorcerer’s Apprentice Camille Saint-Saëns – Cello Concerto No. 1 in A minor Vasily Popov, cello Camille Saint-Saëns – Symphony No. 3 in C minor, “Organ Symphony” Michael Murphy, organ The centerpiece is Saint-Saëns’ thrilling Organ Symphony, which integrates the pipe organ into two of its four movements for a powerful blend of orchestral color and majestic organ sound. Performing on the St. Andrew Pipe Organ of the Holy Archangels—a French Romantic instrument installed by the Peragallo Pipe Organ Company in 2020 (three manuals, 51 ranks, 2,891 pipes)—organist Michael Murphy will bring the work’s full intended glory to life. The program opens with Dukas’ vivid symphonic poem, famously featured in Disney’s Fantasia, followed by one of the most beloved cello concertos of the 19th century. This concert is ideal for anyone who appreciates masterful composition, virtuoso performance, and the transcendent beauty of live symphonic music in a sacred setting. About the Conductor Maestro Simeone Tartaglione is Associate Professor of Practice in Instrumental Music at The Catholic University of America’s Rome School of Performing Arts, where he serves as Conducting Area Head and conductor of the university orchestra. Trained in the European tradition at Rome’s Santa Cecilia Conservatory and with advanced degrees including a Doctorate in Philology, he has conducted across Europe, the United States, South Africa, and beyond. He currently serves as Music Director of the Newark Symphony Orchestra and Delaware Youth Symphony, among others. He is the recipient of the prestigious 2025 Telamone Prize. events.title: Alexandria Association Lecture Marta McDowell, "All the Presidents' Gardens"
events.venue: Alexandria History Museum at the Lyceum
events.description: The White House grounds have mirrored American garden history. Changes to its gardens over time reflect changing fashions in horticulture and design. George Washington employed Pierre Charles L’Enfant who brought a French classical aesthetic to the original site selection. Thomas Jefferson, with the help of architect Benjamin Latrobe, introduced an English romantic sensibility to the South Lawn. In its two-hundred-plus years of history, the White House has had rows of vegetables, extensive glasshouses, Victorian carpet bedding, and styles ranging from Colonial Revival, to Italianate, to the elegant horticultural palette of the Rose Garden. Because the presidents and first ladies want to show the best that the country has to offer, many luminaries of American garden history shaped the eighteen acres that surround the White House. Beatrix Jones Farrand designed a garden for Mrs. Wilson. Andrew Jackson Downing made recommendations to President Fillmore. Frederick Law Olmsted, Jr. wrote a landscape plan for Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Michael Van Valkenburgh and his firm, MVVA, redesigned the Pennsylvania Avenue entrance between 2002 and 2004. events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. events.title: Taiwan Conference: Bilateral Ballot Boxes: U.S. Midterms, Taiwan’s Local Elections, and Policy Trajectories
events.description: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections and Taiwan’s 2026 local elections unfold during landmark democratic anniversaries: the United States’ semiquincentennial and the 30th anniversary of Taiwan’s first direct presidential election. These parallel milestones provide a unique lens for examining how democratic identity, institutional resilience, and cross‑Strait geopolitics shape electoral behavior in both polities. In the United States, midterm dynamics reflect heightened economic anxieties, rising consumer prices, shifting partisan narratives, and growing voter concerns over affordability and foreign policy crises, including the conflict with Iran. Simultaneously, Taiwan’s local elections occur amid intensified political competition, partisan division, heightened public and legislative debate on issues such as defense spending, and renewed attention to democratic consolidation and public trust. U.S.–Taiwan relations increasingly intersect with both electoral contexts. In Washington, bipartisan congressional resolutions reaffirm support for Taiwan’s democratic resilience and highlight growing concern over coercive pressure from the PRC. In Taiwan, cross‑Strait tensions, security and economic relations with the United States, and China’s influence operations—including AI‑driven disinformation—shape public discourse and electoral priorities. events.description: In this talk, Dr. Ekaterina Khodzhaeva will examine how routine criminal law enforcement in Russia has changed since 2022 across all its main levels, from the police and pre-trial investigation to the courts and sentencing. She will focus on changes directly linked to the war and longer- term trends in Russian criminal justice that began earlier and continued after February 2022. Dr. Khodzhaeva will show which processes in the work of the police, investigators and courts continue earlier institutional dynamics, and where wartime has become a factor in its own right that has changed the structure and practices of the criminal justice system.

events.title: Book Launch: Transitional Shakespeare, Gender and Adaption
events.description: Join us for a book launch celebrating Professor of English Alexa Alice Joubin's new book, Transitional Shakespeare, Gender, and Adaption. About the Book The cross-gender role is a staple of Shakespeare’s plays, and drama is a transitional art. Gender is made flesh and brought into being by actors’ embodiment. Similarly, adaptations also operate transitionally. Some adaptations translate narratives into hospitable forms of expression. Other adaptations function as minor uses of established genres and gender categories. In Transitional Shakespeare, Gender, and Adaption, Professor Alexa Alice Joubin, PhD, theorizes “transness” in a number of modes, including composite figures in drama that arise from the convergence of a character, their curated self-image, and actors’ performance; cultural translation; stagecraft onscreen; and drama as processes of social assemblage. Joubin close-reads a number of films, such as Stage Beauty (2004), As We Like It (Taiwan, 2001), The King and the Clown ( South Korea, 2005), She’s the Man (2006) and Shakespeare in Love (1998). RSVP online >> This event is co-sponsored by the Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Studies Program and the Department of English.

events.title: Dragon Falls: Agentic AI and book signing with author Bob Gourley
events.description: GreenFare Organic Cafe presents Dragon Falls: Agentic AI and Book Signing with Author Bob Gourley on Monday, November 17th, 2026 from 5:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. at 408 Elden Street in Herndon, Fairfax County, Virginia. Join your community for dinner from 5:00–5:30 p.m.; the author lecture begins at 6:00 p.m. Dragon Falls isn't just a thriller—it's an insider's view of how cyber warfare and high-tech attacks are currently threatening our world. Retired Navy Commander Jack Tanner arrives in Malaysia on a cybersecurity book tour only to discover that Beijing's shadow war is far more sophisticated than anyone imagined. The Chinese Ministry of State Security and their cyber operatives, known as the Three Immortals, orchestrate a devastating espionage campaign combining intelligence, financial manipulation, autonomous drone swarms, and jungle-based insurgents to destabilize Southeast Asia's strongest democracy. Dragon Falls delivers the complexity of Ludlum-inspired spy conspiracies with Clancy-style techno-thriller sophistication, revealing how today's real technologies are reshaping global conflict. This is the warfare we must master if our way of life is to endure. Brad Meltzer, bestselling author of The Viper, calls it "terrifying and utterly authentic." Shyam Sankar, CTO of Palantir, praises it as "a rare thriller that actually understands the battlefield" with tradecraft that is "real, sequences spot on, and stakes exactly where they should be: on America's need to understand Beijing's shadow war." Bob Gourley, the author, brings expertise from his career in cybersecurity and national security affairs, offering authentic insights into modern espionage and cyber warfare. Meet the author, purchase Dragon Falls, and have it signed following the lecture. Dragon Falls: Agentic AI and Book Signing combines thrilling storytelling, national security education, and community connection in Fairfax County, Virginia. Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: GWSB | Faculty Perspectives & Alumni Connections: Prof. Margaret Ormiston
events.description: Faculty Perspectives & Alumni Connections: Professor Margaret Ormiston (Arlington‚ VA)Topic: How the Questions We Ask Shape the Leaders We SeeLocation UPSIDE on Moore - Coral Room 1700 N. Moore St. Level M2 Arlington‚ VA 22209 UPSIDE on Moore is conveniently located above the Rosslyn Metro station‚ with free garage parking after 6 p.m. (see website for details). Event DescriptionConnect with fellow GW alumni over light hors d’oeuvres and conversation at UPSIDE on Moore in Rosslyn‚ featuring a thought-provoking discussion with GW School of Business Professor Margaret Ormiston. Bar service and soft drinks will be available. We tend to think questions help us learn about others. But what if the questions we ask also shape what we see? Drawing on research examining thousands of exchanges between journalists and CEOs‚ Professor Ormiston will explore how male and female leaders are asked different questions‚ how those questions influence their answers‚ and how those answers shape perceptions of their leadership. Discover what these findings reveal about gender bias and the questions we ask and answer in our own professional lives. Enjoy networking before and after a brief faculty presentation and audience Q&A. Registration includes light hors d’oeuvres‚ soft drinks‚ and two drink tickets. Reserve your spot for an evening of alumni connections and fresh perspectives on leadership!

events.title: Jesse Cook
events.description: A global artist in every sense of the word, Jesse Cook redefines music’s power to connect people across cultures and continents. Over the last three decades, the Paris-born, Toronto-raised master of the Spanish guitar has built a devoted following for his spellbinding rumba flamenco, routinely selling out performance halls from London to Los Angeles, Milan to Montreal. On stage, Cook radiates infectious energy, collaborating with his band and guest instrumentalists to craft immersive, unforgettable experiences. His concerts are celebrated for their warmth, precision, and emotional depth. Throughout his decades-long career, Jesse Cook has remained devoted to musical exploration. His boundary-defying artistry has introduced flamenco and world music to wider audiences while maintaining a signature style that is both technically masterful and soulfully expressive. That authenticity has clearly resonated—with over a billion streams and views across platforms to date—proving his sound remains as relevant as it is revered.

Based on Victor Hugo’s sweeping 19th-century novel of redemption, revolution, and love, the songs of Les Miz conquered Broadway in the 1980s and continue to resonate in this third decade of the 21st Century. Follow Jean-Valjean from his beginnings as convict #24601 to life in hiding, to protector of Cosette, pursued all the while by the relentless Javert, culminating in the revolutionary passions of the 1832 Paris uprising. Join us at the barricade this holiday season, and be stirred by a musical unmatched by its lyrical humor, its calls for justice, and its portrayal of the sacrifices one can make in the name of love. Featuring: Kevin S. McAllister as Javert, Alex De Bard as Eponine, Tracy Lynn Olivera as Madame Thénardier, Jordan Friend as Thénardier, Stephanie Waters as Fantine, Ben Clark as Marius, and more to be announced soon.

events.description: The Folk Club of Reston-Herndon welcomes YouTube sensation Mean Mary to the Amphora Diner Deluxe (1151 Elden St.) this coming Tuesday November 17th at 7:00 pm. Her latest album, Woman Creature (Portrait of a Woman, Part 2) , was named Country Music Peoples #1 Critics' Choice Album of 2024, and her recording of "Wayfaring Stranger" was recently featured in the feature film Hellfire. Deering Banjos named her their Goodtime Ambassador, and Janet Deering describes Mary's banjo playing as giving her "chills." Equally versatile on guitar, fiddle, and eight other instruments. events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Nick Moss Band
events.description: Since first forming The Nick Moss Band featuring Dennis Gruenling in 2016, master blues guitarist Nick Moss and world-class harmonica virtuoso Dennis Gruenling have become torchbearers for traditional electric blues. But rather than simply repeating what’s come before, the band’s high-energy take on old school Chicago, Texas and West Coast sounds is completely their own. With their new Alligator Records release (their third for the label), Get Your Back Into It!, Chicago native Moss and New Jersey native Gruenling—together with Rodrigo Mantovani on bass, and Pierce Downer on drums—deliver a deeply rooted, timeless blue collar blues album. AllMusic says the band, winners of the 2020 & 2024 Blues Music Award for Blues Band Of The Year, “makes the case for the vitality of old-fashioned Chicago electric blues in the 21st century.” They are among the world’s very best old school blues ensembles, with each musician expertly playing off the others. “We are a rare breed as far as how authentic we like to keep the music, while also keeping it up-to-date and exciting,” says Moss. Among many awards and recognitions the band has received, Nick Moss garnered the 2019 Blues Music Award for Best Traditional Blues Male Artist. The band took home Blues Music Awards in 2020 for Album of the Year, Song of the Year, and Band of the Year. In 2024 the band received the prestigious Band of the Year honors again from the Blues Music Awards. Bandmates Dennis Gruenling and Rodrigo Mantovani have been nominated multiple times in their respective categories for instrumentalist harmonica and bass. Dennis also received the award for Best Harmonica Instrumentalist in 2019. Nick Moss proudly represents the city of Chicago as one of the few bluesmen working today to have learned his craft firsthand, directly from many of the genre’s original creators…and rest assured that the band will bring you the best in authentic Blues! Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Nuclear Risks and Regional Stability in the Middle East
events.description: The Middle East Policy Forum, in partnership with the Institute for Security and Conflict Studies, welcomes Professor Sina Azodi, Ambassador (ret.) Bonnie Jenkins, and subject area expert Ms. Clara Sherwood, to discuss Nuclear Risks and Regional Stability in the Middle East. The Middle East nuclear debate has never been more relevant than it is in 2026. To discuss this issue, our panelists will examine regional and global attitudes towards nuclear weapons in the Middle East, with an eye toward generating conclusions and strategies regarding the future of non-proliferation in the region. This distinguished panel includes Professor Sina Azodi, a renowned Iran expert whose recent book, Iran and the Bomb, offers one of the most in-depth examinations of the Iranian nuclear program to date. Joining Professor Azodi is Ambassador (ret.) Bonnie Jenkins, the former Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security from 2021-2024 and current Elliott School Shapiro Visiting Professor of International Affairs. Rounding out the panel is Ms. Clara Sherwood, Executive Director at the National Nuclear Security Administration and a foreign affairs specialist with experience across U.S. government agencies, think tanks, and international programs. We hope you will join the Middle East Policy Forum and the Institute for Security and Conflict Studies to discuss Nuclear Risks and Regional Stability in the Middle East. This event is open to the general public and the media. Copie

events.title: Profs & Pints Annapolis: How Ancient Athens Restored Democracy
events.description: Profs and Pints Annapolis presents: “How Ancient Athens Restored Democracy,” on lessons to be learned from an overthrow of tyrants in 403 B.C., with Nicholas D. Cross, assistant professor of history at the United States Naval Academy and author of The Roots of Cooperation: Constructing Interstate Alliances in Ancient Greece. The defeat of Athens in the Peloponnesian War led to its democracy being replaced by the Thirty Tyrants, an oligarchic regime that consolidated power through executions and political repression. Democratic exiles managed to organize resistance, defeat the oligarchic forces, and return to Athens to restore democratic government, but then faced the far more challenging task of reconciling a community torn apart by political divisions. The restorers of Athenian democracy grappled with a question that often arises in periods of political upheaval: Can a deeply divided community ever overcome its past and build a shared future? Learn how they managed to bring about such an outcome in a talk that holds hopeful lessons for our own time. The speaker, Dr. Nicholas Cross, teaches the history of ancient Greece and Rome and is the author of a forthcoming biography of the leader of democratic resistance to the Thirty Tyrants, Thrasybulus of Steiria: An Athenian Hero? He’ll describe how the settlement that followed the civil war included an amnesty designed to prevent cycles of retaliation, but Athens nonetheless remained deeply divided. Among those who had to find a way to live together once more were former democrats, supporters of oligarchy, and citizens such as Socrates whose conduct during the regime was open to question. Democracy’s return was not a straightforward triumph. It instead involved dealing with tensions and making political decisions intended to enable peaceful coexistence possible. Renowned storyteller and cultural educator Dovie Thomason presents a special on-stage educational performance celebrating Native American Heritage Month. As we prepare for Thanksgiving, Stories of Thanks shares the tales of many cultures explaining the original “whys” of the world, as science does now. The imagery and values in the stories from Dovie’s Native ancestry pair the “whys” of science with the very contemporary “hows” of living in balance on our shared Earth. This enriching experience supports learning through the arts while inspiring students to listen deeply, celebrate heritage, and appreciate the power of stories passed down through generations.

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. events.title: Deer Tick w/ DUG
events.description: The ninth studio album from Deer Tick, Coin-O-Matic casts a bright light on a little-known facet of the American mythos: the hidden histories of the band’s home state of Rhode Island, where the everyday dramas of working-class families long collided with the menace of the mafia underworld. As they tapped into their infinite fascination with that strange duality, singer/guitarist John McCauley, guitarist/singer Ian O’Neil, drummer/singer Dennis Ryan, and bassist Christopher Ryan assembled a batch of songs exploring desperation, grief, redemption, and resilience with both cinematic detail and lived-in emotionality. A sharp new turn from one of indie-rock’s most enduringly vital forces, Coin-O-Matic arrives as a complicated love letter to a way of life slowly slipping from the collective memory.

events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: South Lakes Theatre Arts Presents Come From Away
events.description: South Lakes Theatre Arts Presents Come From Away First Responders and Open Captions Show Come From Away, written by Irene Sankoff and David Hein, is a critically acclaimed musical featuring a poignantly relevant script and a deeply moving score. The show’s global presence resonates across all audiences as an uplifting reminder of humanity’s ability to come together, no matter what the circumstances. Based on real events of September 11th, 2001, Come From Away tells the story in which 38 planes, carrying thousands of passengers from across the globe, were diverted to the isolated community of Gander, Newfoundland. The locals of the small town played host to the world as they fed, housed, and comforted the stranded passengers for over four days. Inundated by culture clashes and language barriers, the people of Gander persevered, demonstrating the power of kindness. On the 10 th anniversary of 9/11 in 2011, Sankoff and Hein traveled to Gander to interview residents and returning passengers. They turned hundreds of distinct accounts into a celebrated musical. For this 25 th anniversary year of September 11th, South Lakes Theatre Arts is honored to bring these accounts to life. Content Warning: Some mature content & langage.

events.title: Speaking Truth to Power: The Free Press in a Changing World
events.description: Presented by the MD Two-Fifty Commission. Join us for a special evening of programming and a community conversation about the state of journalism and a free press in the United States. Two hundred fifty years ago, the founders of our country believed that a free press was essential to building and keeping a successful democracy. Freedom of the press, along with freedom of speech, freedom of religion, and the freedom to peacefully assemble and to petition the government, are rights protected by the First Amendment. Yet today, as we celebrate the 250th anniversary of our country’s founding, Americans are watching struggles between the government and the press over exactly what a free press means. Citizens are concerned about court rulings, lawsuits, Justice Department investigations, governmental banning of reporters from news coverage, anti-press statements from government officials, and attacks against journalists. On international surveys, America’s ranking as a country with a free press has dropped significantly. Citizens are left wondering who qualifies as “the press.” Who can citizens trust? What does the future of a free press in America look like in these times? This event brings together an experienced group of journalists to offer insight into these questions. As our keynote speaker, Terry Moran will address these issues head-on. Attendees can also view the “Revolutionary Maryland: Freedom of the Press Then and Now” exhibition. This community event comes at a crucial point in time, as Americans are watching struggles between the government and the press over exactly what a free press means in 2026. Dubbed a “master of musical imagination” by NPR’s World Café Live and “astonishing” by WBUR Boston, Lorenz’s weathered, howl-flecked voice was described by Rochester City Newspaper as “a cross between Hound Dog Taylor and a Tuvan throat singer who has swallowed a bird.” Lorenz has earned snowballing acclaim for his achingly poetic dark folk. A solitary artist with an organic yet ornate vision, his seventh album To Go On is his most acutely profound yet. Created in the wake of losing his sister, singer-songwriter Kate Lorenz, it’s a tender, beautiful, and arrestingly moving record; an internal dialogue and conversation with the departed, enormously resonant to anyone who ever loved anyone. events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Blitzkid
events.description: Horror punk legends BLITZKID return to the road this fall in support of their long-awaited new studio album, MODERN HEL, their first full length release in sixteen years. Formed in 1997, Blitzkid quickly became one of the most influential bands in modern horror punk and has remained one of the genre’s leading exponents. Known for their driving punk energy, dark atmosphere, and unforgettable melodic hooks, the band has built an international following through decades of touring across the globe. From Wave Gotik Treffen to Wacken Open Air, Blitzkid’s versatility has allowed them to perform at some of the world’s most notable genre festivals, demonstrating the band’s unique ability to connect with audiences across multiple underground scenes. With MODERN HEL, Blitzkid enters a powerful new chapter. While the band’s signature haunting melodies and anthemic choruses remain firmly intact, the new material pushes their sound into more aggressive territory, incorporating a blistering fusion of thrash and hardcore to a degree the band has never explored before. The result is a blistering blend of driving riffs and haunting hooks that have defined Blitzkid for nearly three decades. MODERN HE

events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: CENTENNIAL FILM Series: Cabin in the Sky (1943)
events.description: A Musical Battle Between Good & Evil Cabin in the Sky follows Little Joe, a man who, after being killed over gambling debts, awakens in purgatory and is granted six months back on Earth to redeem himself and prove he deserves entry into Heaven. His journey through faith, love, and moral conflict unfolds through a series of musical performances that reflect both earthly temptation and heavenly intervention. Featuring music by Duke Ellington and his Orchestra , Cabin in the Sky blends gospel, jazz, and theatrical storytelling into a rich stylized musical fantasy. The film is notable for its all-Black cast, making it an important early example of mainstream Hollywood representation during the Golden Age of cinema. Combining vivid fantasy sequences, moral allegory, and elaborate musical staging, Cabin in the Sky remains a visually striking and culturally significant work celebrated for its artistry, performances, and lasting historical importance. STARS: Lena Horne, Ethel Waters, Eddie Anderson, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong RUNTIME: 97 minutes GENRE: Musical, Comedy This show is part of the Weinberg Center’s Centennial Film Event, celebrating 100 years of screenings in our historic building. The Weinberg Center , located in the heart of Downtown Frederick, MD, offers a historic backdrop and timeless atmosphere for a unique film experience.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Forest Germans between Geography, History and Memory: Mapping a Forgotten Settlement Region in Southern Poland
events.description: One of the most intriguing paradoxes in Central European history is that a Polish cultural and territorial community is known as the Forest Germans, a name reflecting the complexity of its identity and history. The Forest Germans emerged through centuries of cultural and biological synthesis, combining German influences with West Slavic and, above all, Polish elements. Their history dates back to the 14th century, when medieval German newcomers and West Slavic settlers from Germania Slavica, through intermingling with the Polish population, gradually underwent complete Polonization between the 16th and 18th centuries. Through assimilation, acculturation, adaptation, and cultural exchange, the Forest Germans emerged as a distinct cultural group in Poland not later than in the 17th century. Today, their descendants live in the northern Carpathians in south-eastern Poland, where Polish and German surnames, place names, and family histories intertwine. Marcin Wojciech Solarz, PhD, the IR researcher at the Faculty of Geography and Regional Studies of the University of Warsaw, Poland will give a lecture examining the history, ethnonym, and settlement boundaries of Forest Germany. He distinguishes the broader region, known as Great Forest Germany, from the narrower settlement area, Small Forest Germany, divided into at least three settlement enclaves: Biecz, Krosno, and Łańcut. events.description: High Tea with the Highlands: A Bridgerton-Inspired Tea Party + Highland Cow + Lamb Affair ​ ​Dearest Gentle Readers, It would appear that the ladies of Scarlet Springs Farm have once again orchestrated an affair most enchanting. events.title: Mental Reset: Sound Bath + Reiki : Thursday Evenings in Falls Church
events.address: 7777 Leesburg Pike, Ste 204S, Falls Church, VA 22043
events.description: Thursday is a weird day. The week isn't over, but you are. Mental Reset is one hour at the end of the workday where nobody needs anything from you. You come in, you lie down on a mat, you get a blanket and a bolster, and for the next sixty minutes your only job is to listen. I play crystal singing bowls, guide you through a short meditation so your mind has something to do besides replay the day, and offer Reiki while you rest. Most people tell me some version of the same thing afterward: the noise in their head finally turned down. Not off: down. Enough that they can go home and actually be home, instead of answering emails in their head at the dinner table. You don't need experience. You don't need to know how to meditate, and you definitely don't need to “clear your mind.” If you could do that, you wouldn't need this class. First-timers are in the room most weeks. There are ten spots. That's deliberate. It's a small room, I can see everyone in it, and it never feels like an event. It feels like an exhale. A few regulars started as skeptics; more than one of our Google reviews comes from someone who arrived doubting the whole thing and left surprised at how settled they felt. You don't have to believe in anything for an hour of sound and rest to do you some good. Run by Victoria Vita: CPA for 20+ years, healer for 7+. I sat behind a desk with a brain that wouldn't switch off for a long time before I found this work. Thursday nights are built for the person I used to be. Rated 5.0 from 32 Google reviews. Come straight from work. Leave like the week let go of you first. What's included: • 60 minutes of crystal singing bowls, guided meditation and Reiki • Mat, blanket, and bolster everything is here; you bring nothing • Small group: 10 people maximum, same teacher every week • Time at the end to sit up slowly, have water, and not rush out Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: One Moses, Two Scriptures: The Torah and the Qur'an in Conversation
events.description: The Torah and the Qur'an tell stories about many of the same figures — above all, Moses, the prophet the Qur'an names more often than any other. For fourteen centuries, Jews and Muslims have interpreted these stories through traditions in each other's shadow, amid rivalry, exchange and mutual influence. What happens when they are read side by side? Join GW's Ambassador John L. Loeb, Jr. Institute for Religious Freedom and Democracy for a discussion about what the two scriptures share, where they diverge and what reading them together can — and cannot — do for Jews and Muslims today. Speakers: Rick Sopher (Woolf Institute) is co-author (with Abdulla Galadari) of the recently published Illuminating Scriptural Connections: A Qur'anic Commentary on the Torah (Jewish Publication Society, 2026), which reads every weekly Torah portion alongside the Qur'an.Mustafa Akyol (Cato Institute), author of The Islamic Moses: How the Prophet Inspired Jews and Muslims to Flourish Together and Change the World (St. Martin's, 2024), has explored the common religious grammar of law, prophecy and scholarship that has connected Judaism and Islam across the centuries.Historian of Islam Joel Blecher, associate professor of history at George Washington University, is a scholar of Islamic intellectual history and traditions of textual interpretation.RSVP >>

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: South Lakes Theatre Arts Presents Come From Away
events.description: Come From Away, written by Irene Sankoff and David Hein, is a critically acclaimed musical featuring a poignantly relevant script and a deeply moving score. The show’s global presence resonates across all audiences as an uplifting reminder of humanity’s ability to come together, no matter what the circumstances. Based on real events of September 11th, 2001, Come From Away tells the story in which 38 planes, carrying thousands of passengers from across the globe, were diverted to the isolated community of Gander, Newfoundland. The locals of the small town played host to the world as they fed, housed, and comforted the stranded passengers for over four days. Inundated by culture clashes and language barriers, the people of Gander persevered, demonstrating the power of kindness. On the 10 th anniversary of 9/11 in 2011, Sankoff and Hein traveled to Gander to interview residents and returning passengers. They turned hundreds of distinct accounts into a celebrated musical. For this 25 th anniversary year of September 11th, South Lakes Theatre Arts is honored to bring these accounts to life.

Read more about the exhibitions below: Unfossilizing African Art: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.description: The Battle of Tarawa was a strategic victory for the United States in November 1943, but it came at a heavy cost. events.title: The Great War and Great Flu Come to the Mother Continent
events.address: 400 Ferndale Ave., Hodson Auditorium, Rosenstock Hall, Frederick, MD 21701
events.description: The First World War began in Africa on Aug 3, 1914, six days after hostilities began in Europe. Across the continent, the miserable yoke of European imperialism was felt by local people forced into a conflict they did not ask for. Join us for an immersive historical evening exploring one of World War I’s most grueling theaters. We will screen “Chasing the Phantom”, a 2007 Lucasfilm documentary that follows the legendary campaign of German General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, the "Lion of Africa", who led a guerrilla campaign with African askaris through German East Africa. His forces evaded capture throughout the war, surrendering only two weeks after the 1918 Armistice. Scott Hileman Ph.D. will begin the evening with an overview of the African theater. After the film, we will discuss WWI’s devastating impact on the continent, including the 1918 influenza pandemic, with historians Anne Samson Ph.D. and Peter Doyle, Ph.D. The Great Flu would inflict a terrible toll on both the Lion’s malnourished troops and on the African peoples, one often overlooked in tales of WWI. Hosted by Department of Biology as part of International Education Week 2026. Co-sponsored by Center for Global Studies & the Graduate School. Refreshments will be provided. Admission is free and open to all. Please RSVP to Mark Chee Ph.D., chee@hood.edu Can't join us in person? Please register for a Zoom invitation at https://tinyurl.com/mph-film-fest

events.title: The Importance of Climate Leadership and the Power of Public Action
events.description: Al Gore and Rep. Maxwell Frost discuss climate, democracy, affordability and their hopes for the future. Twenty years ago, former Vice President Al Gore and The Climate Reality Project set out to turn everyday citizens into leaders. Today, we find ourselves posing the question: with a new Congress, will there be fresh opportunities for progress? This is an in-person event. No livestream will be available. Vice President Gore, who has spent decades pushing the climate crisis to the center of public debate, is joined by Congressman Maxwell Frost, a longtime organizer who brings the urgency of a new generation to Capitol Hill. Together, they’ll hold a cross-generational conversation on the road ahead: the policy priorities facing lawmakers, the payoffs clean energy is already delivering, and the ways an engaged citizenry and organizations like Climate Reality are standing up to the fossil fuel industry and turning ambition into change.

events.description: Join Free Minds Book Club & Writing Workshop for a special advance screening of “Verses from the Inside,” an episode from The Poet Speaks Season 2: We Speak What Was , ahead of its broadcast premiere on PBS and Heritage Broadcasting. A conversation follows the screening with Free Minds poets and host Amanda Eke. About the Episode Episode 2, “Verses from the Inside,” follows host Amanda Eke inside a Washington, D.C. correctional facility, where poetry becomes a lifeline, a way to process, reflect, and reclaim a voice in a place designed to take so much of that voice away. The episode then follows Free Minds poets who have carried that practice beyond incarceration and into their lives as artists and advocates. From inside the walls to life beyond them, Verses from the Inside asks what poetry can make possible when words become a means of survival, connection, and transformation. About the Series The Poet Speaks is a documentary-style series hosted by Amanda Eke that explores the power of poetry as a cultural and historical force. Season 2, We Speak What Was , is a six-episode journey through Washington, D.C., where poetry, music, memory, history, and community collide. Support Free Minds This event is free and open to all. A donation alone does not reserve a seat. To attend and support Free Minds Book Club & Writing Workshop, select both a free admission ticket and an optional donation.

events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.description: Virginia helped shape the beginnings of our nation, and local audiences can experience the drama, humor and music behind America’s founding in 1776 , the Tony Award-winning musical presented by The Pickwick Players. Just in time for America’s 250th anniversary, 1776 takes audiences inside the Continental Congress, where John Adams pushes for independence, Benjamin Franklin brings his wit and wisdom, and Virginia’s own Thomas Jefferson is called upon to put the revolutionary cause into words. The story also features Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, whose resolution calling for independence helped move the colonies toward a historic decision. What happens when a room full of passionate, stubborn and politically divided men try to agree on the future of a nation? There’s plenty of debate, a little scheming, larger-than-life personalities and some unforgettable music. With music and lyrics by Sherman Edwards and a book by Peter Stone, 1776 combines clever dialogue, colorful characters, political maneuvering and a memorable score. From the spirited opening number, “Sit Down, John,” to the lively “The Lees of Old Virginia” and the stirring “Is Anybody There?,” the music captures the humor, frustrations and high stakes behind the birth of a nation. Forget the dusty history books. 1776 presents the founding fathers as real people, with big egos, strong opinions, competing interests and a monumental decision to make. events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. As the singing and celebration give way to confrontation, old wounds reopen and new revelations emerge. Leslye Headland’s “stormy, compassionate, [and] cuttingly observant” ( TimeOut NY ) play interrogates the complexity of family loyalty, the power of religion, and what it truly means to love one another.

events.title: Disney Frozen the Broadway Musical

Along the way, Anna teams up with rugged ice harvester Kristoff, his loyal reindeer Sven, and the ever-optimistic snowman Olaf in an adventure that tests the meaning of love, loyalty, and sacrifice. Featuring dazzling costumes, spectacular scenic effects, and expanded storytelling created especially for the stage, Frozen goes beyond the film to deepen the bond between the sisters at its core. The musical includes beloved songs such as “Let It Go,” “Do You Want to Build a Snowman?” and “For the First Time in Forever,” alongside thrilling new numbers written exclusively for Broadway. A powerful tale of self-acceptance and the unbreakable strength of family, Frozen the Broadway Musical is a magical, uplifting experience for audiences of all ages. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Gallery B Presents “Intersections | Realism & Abstraction”
events.description: “ INTERSECTIONS ⎸ Realism & Abstraction” is a group exhibition featuring four artists – Lawrence Chandler, Angela Iovino, Ariana Progri, and Ravi Raman – with distinct art styles in conversation with each other, showing that even the most realistic art is a form of abstraction (a reduction of reality) and that abstract art can hold elements of structural, grounded reality. Instead of treating realism and abstraction as binary opposites, works in the exhibition also intersect both worlds, showcasing how different artists navigate the spectrum between the two styles. Viewers not only will see realistic figures and recognizable subjects dissolving into, or emerging from abstract backgrounds, but also the use of bold brushstrokes, form, color, and textures to convey emotion rather than literal details.

events.title: Lonesome River Band
events.description: It’s hard to think of a genre more committed to sustained creative careers than bluegrass. Case in point: the 41-years-and-counting path of Mountain Home Music Company stalwarts, Lonesome River Band. Though the last remaining original member departed before the turn of the century, the group — a quintet for more than 20 years now — hasn’t so much reinvented itself as refined a profoundly influential signature sound that has a seemingly endless appeal to successive generations of fans and musicians alike. Led by 30-plus year veteran and award-winning banjo man Sammy Shelor, who has presided over one stellar lineup after another, LRB remains among the genre’s most widely admired and powerful draws, both in person and on streaming platforms.

events.title: Michael McDermott
events.description: Jammin' Java welcomes singer-songwriter Michael McDermott on Thursday, November 20th, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. at 227 Maple Avenue in Vienna, Fairfax County, Virginia. Chicago native McDermott has occupied a peculiar and essential place in American music for thirty-plus years: extravagantly praised by Stephen King, The Washington Post, and The Hollywood Reporter, yet perpetually on the verge of the recognition his artistry demands. Raised on the dual gospel of early Dylan and the Stones, Tom Waits and the Who, Woody Guthrie and Van Morrison, McDermott has never made a record that fits neatly into a marketing category—a restless refusal to be contained that makes him essential. His forthcoming album Flowers From The Graveyard (arriving August 21, 2027) collects 11 self-penned songs moving fluidly between anthemic rock and bruised introspection, between political fury and hard-won philosophical calm. The Hollywood Reporter notes "Despair never sounded so good," while Stephen King calls him "one of the best songwriters in the world." The Washington Post suggests "McDermott may prove to be one of his generation's greatest talents." This intimate performance delivers the uncompromising songwriting, raw emotional depth, and masterful artistry that define one of America's most important voices. Admission is $34.00 plus fees. Michael McDermott combines lyrical excellence, unflinching humanity, and timeless rock 'n' roll soul in Fairfax County, Virginia. Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.description: Calling all filmmakers, screenwriters, producers, directors, cinematographers, editors, and film students! The PGFF Take 5 Industry Masterclasses bring together industry insights, creative expertise, and emerging technologies to help you sharpen your craft and prepare for what’s next. Join us Friday, November 20, 2026, at Bowie State University for five masterclasses designed to inspire your next project and expand your creative toolkit. One Day. Five Masterclasses. The State of Film: Navigating Hollywood’s New Era Explore how studio mergers, streaming, AI, and changing audience habits are reshaping the industry with actor and author Derrick A. King. Crafting Sanctuary: The Art, Integrity, and Collaboration of The Barber Go behind the scenes to discover how writing, performance, cinematography, sound, and production come together to bring a powerful story to life. The Writer’s Edge: Crafting Stories That Get Noticed Screenwriter and producer Tressa Azarel Smallwood, Founder and CEO of MegaMind Media, shares insights to help writers strengthen their storytelling and develop standout scripts. From Script to Screen: Virtual Production and AI in the Modern Filmmaker’s Workflow Explore how virtual production and AI are transforming filmmaking, from previsualization to production and post-production. Soul in Motion: Experience the Magic of Motion Capture Discover how motion capture expands creative possibilities across film, animation, gaming, and virtual production.

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: South Lakes Theatre Arts Presents Come From Away
events.description: Come From Away, written by Irene Sankoff and David Hein, is a critically acclaimed musical featuring a poignantly relevant script and a deeply moving score. The show’s global presence resonates across all audiences as an uplifting reminder of humanity’s ability to come together, no matter what the circumstances. Based on real events of September 11th, 2001, Come From Away tells the story in which 38 planes, carrying thousands of passengers from across the globe, were diverted to the isolated community of Gander, Newfoundland. The locals of the small town played host to the world as they fed, housed, and comforted the stranded passengers for over four days. Inundated by culture clashes and language barriers, the people of Gander persevered, demonstrating the power of kindness. On the 10 th anniversary of 9/11 in 2011, Sankoff and Hein traveled to Gander to interview residents and returning passengers. They turned hundreds of distinct accounts into a celebrated musical. For this 25 th anniversary year of September 11th, South Lakes Theatre Arts is honored to bring these accounts to life. Content Warning: Some mature content & langage. Disclaimer: There will be NO intermission for this production.

events.title: Transgender Day of Remembrance and Resilience (TDORR)
events.description: Friday, November 20th—Join us for Trans Day of Remembrance and Resilience (TDORR), a day of COMMUNITY POWER when we honor the memories of transgender people whose lives were lost in acts of violence this year. What is TDOR? From GLAAD : the first Transgender Day of Remembrance (TDOR) was started in 1999 by transgender advocate Gwendolyn Ann Smith as a vigil to honor the memory of Rita Hester, a transgender woman killed in 1998. The vigil commemorated all the transgender people lost to violence since Rita Hester’s death, and began an important tradition that has become the annual Transgender Day of Remembrance. In a 2012 article with Huffpost , Smith is quoted as saying, “the right to simply exist is first and foremost. With so many seeking to erase transgender people — sometimes in the most brutal ways possible — it is vitally important that those we lose are remembered, and that we continue to fight for justice.” Why the 2nd “R”? While not entirely widespread (yet), the MoCo Pride Family uses the moniker “TDORR” to underscore gratitude as essential to our celebration of transgender lives. On the Transgender Day of Remembrance, we honor those we have lost and those that continue to live in the face of violence, oppression, and all other forces turned against our community. Transgender people are brave — we will survive, and we will do so with our ancestors and martyrs in our hearts. events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.title: 1776, the Musical, presented by The Pickwick Players
events.description: Virginia helped shape the beginnings of our nation, and local audiences can experience the drama, humor and music behind America’s founding in 1776 , the Tony Award-winning musical presented by The Pickwick Players. Just in time for America’s 250th anniversary, 1776 takes audiences inside the Continental Congress, where John Adams pushes for independence, Benjamin Franklin brings his wit and wisdom, and Virginia’s own Thomas Jefferson is called upon to put the revolutionary cause into words. The story also features Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, whose resolution calling for independence helped move the colonies toward a historic decision. What happens when a room full of passionate, stubborn and politically divided men try to agree on the future of a nation? There’s plenty of debate, a little scheming, larger-than-life personalities and some unforgettable music. With music and lyrics by Sherman Edwards and a book by Peter Stone, 1776 combines clever dialogue, colorful characters, political maneuvering and a memorable score. From the spirited opening number, “Sit Down, John,” to the lively “The Lees of Old Virginia” and the stirring “Is Anybody There?,” the music captures the humor, frustrations and high stakes behind the birth of a nation. Forget the dusty history books. 1776 presents the founding fathers as real people, with big egos, strong opinions, competing interests and a monumental decision to make. events.title: Arts Barn Stage Adventures: The Hollow Stump  Presented by Beech Tree Puppets
events.description: Arts Barn Stage Adventures is a performing arts series for children ages 6 and under, featuring live theatre, music, dance, puppetry, magic, and storytelling. Each performance includes an opportunity to meet and engage with the performing artist, followed by a hands-on creative activity inspired by the show. Designed to spark imagination and bring families together, every event encourages young children to watch, create, play, and explore the arts at the Gaithersburg Arts Barn. In the Hollow Stump presented by Beech Tree Puppets, seven very different animals seek shelter from the winter cold and snow in a large hollow stump. The cuddly, hand-crafted rod-puppets will enchant any child as the characteristics of each animal are revealed through a unique and descriptive poem and song. When the animals let newcomers enter and the space inside the stump grows tighter, these songs interweave. Adapted from the popular tale, The Mitten, this tale celebrates community, as the animals learn to share one space. Gentle and sensory friendly. Join us afterward for a fun, hands‑on activity where kids can carve their own woodland creatures with scratch cards in the Arts Barn Gallery!

events.title: Autumn in Watercolor: A Fall Painting Workshop @ Lost Rhino Brewery
events.description: Spend a cozy fall evening slowing down, sipping, and exploring watercolor at Lost Rhino Brewery! This three-hour beginner-friendly workshop is designed to be a full creative experience, giving you the time to learn, experiment, and complete two fall-inspired paintings: a colorful birch tree landscape and a sweet pumpkin/ gourd “Thankful” card to take home. Led by a professional practicing artist and painter, you’ll be guided step-by-step while learning approachable watercolor techniques along the way. We’ll explore how to work with water and pigment, build layers, create texture, and embrace the beautiful, fluid nature of watercolor. No painting experience is needed, and there will be plenty of room to make each piece feel like your own. More than just leaving with two finished paintings, the goal of this workshop is to give you a foundation you can take with you. You’ll leave with new skills, a better understanding of watercolor, and hopefully a new creative outlet you can continue enjoying long after the class is over. All painting materials are included, plus each ticket includes a beverage from the bar to sip while you paint. Come settle in for three cozy hours of painting, learning, and creating something inspired by the season.

In this festive hands-on workshop, Maria of Beaver Creek Cottage Garden will guide you through crafting a charming collection of handmade ornaments using materials straight from nature. You'll create an adorable snowman couple and a whimsical Christmas fairy — all made from natural materials like dried botanicals, seed pods, twigs, moss, berries, and more. She taught at Tai Sophia (now known as Maryland University of Integrative Health) and Continuing Education at Anne Arundel Community College for over 30 years. events.description: Cocoa, Cookies & Cows | A Highland Cow + Valais Sheep Holiday Experience One of Scarlet Springs Farm’s most beloved holiday traditions is back! Cocoa, Cookies & Cows invites you to spend a festive afternoon with our adorable Highland cows, calves, Valais sheep, and lambs before warming up with homemade hot cocoa and cookies in our beautifully decorated Ridgetop Stable. Your experience begins with a 30-minute group animal immersion, where you’ll have the chance to pet, brush, feed, and love on our friendly Highland cows and calves, along with our famously puppy-dog-friendly Valais sheep and lambs. While the animals don’t mind sharing their barn, this portion of the experience will be largely outdoors, so please dress accordingly. After enjoying the highlands & lambs, we’ll clean up and then head down to the Ridgetop Stable, where you can warm up in our heated, enclosed space for the remaining hour while taking in the sweeping views of the farm. For the holidays, the stable will be transformed with festive décor and music to create the perfect cozy holiday setting. Settle in with your family, sip on homemade hot cocoa, enjoy a tower of delicious cookies, and soak up what makes Scarlet Springs so special. Before you head home, be sure to stop by The Scarlet Shop for Highland-inspired Christmas gifts and keepsakes. Whether this is your first visit or an annual family tradition, Cocoa, Cookies & Cows is the perfect way to slow down, get cozy, and make holiday memories together.​ ​What’s Included with Your Ticket: 1.5 hour experience on the beautiful 74-acre Scarlet Springs Far 30 minutes with the Highlands — pet, brush, feed, and meet our fluffy, friendly Highland cows and calves Time with our Valais sheep and lambs Seat with your party in our festive, beautifully decorated and heated Ridgetop Stable Homemade hot cocoa and cookies Sweeping views of the farm and a festive holiday atmosphere
